scene: She greets me with a quick handshake instead of a hug, then switches hands halfway through like she forgot which one she started with.
She lowers her voice to a whisper whenever she says the word "Tuesday," like it's not allowed today.
She apologizes mid-conversation and steps aside to discreetly adjust her shirt because it’s leaking milk again.
She answers every question from a sideways angle, like when I ask the time she tells me how long until her bus comes.
She talks through her grocery list out loud as we walk, including the things she decided not to buy.
She has a calm way of checking the door lock exactly nine times before we leave.
She sets the jar on the table and tells me it’s her homegrown honey, even though she doesn’t have any bees.
She moves through her morning slowly, setting a timer every ten minutes so she doesn’t accidentally finish anything too quickly.
She has a Middle Eastern look and insists on greeting every new person twice, once when she meets them and again exactly three minutes later.
Her bag hangs slightly open at all times because she says things get restless if you zip them in too long.
She’s wearing a jacket with dozens of small beetle shells sewn into the shoulders.
She’s wearing a baseball cap with a small patch that says it’s part of a local hat union.
Her shoes are tied to exactly the same tightness on both feet, and she reties one if it feels even a little different.
Her style is always the same light layers, like she’s dressed for a mild spring day no matter how cold it actually is.
Her style, even sitting down, is perfectly put together except she keeps both shoes placed neatly side by side under her chair instead of on her feet.
Her style is very square and boxy, and she only wears outfits that match the shape of whatever room she’s going into.
She hangs her jacket on the back of the chair and tucks a small note into its pocket for whoever ends up wearing it next.
She stands under the awning watching the fat rain and waits until exactly thirty drops hit the curb before she'll walk.
She carries a small bucket with a fish in it and says it does better inland.
She crushes a little piece of ash between her fingers and says it keeps men from getting too sure of themselves.
She sets an artichoke on the table like she always does before we start eating anything else.
At the café she winces when someone starts yelling and quietly adds a tally under a notebook page she’s labeled "yelling."
She turns her mug so I can see the bird on it and says it's an alleged loon.
We stop by the dam and she checks the water level against a pencil mark she says moves a little every night.
She wipes the car’s headlight with her sleeve and says it won’t need replacing for another thousand years.
She ties a small bow in her hair and waits a few seconds before speaking, like she’s expecting a signal to start.
She uses an old missile casing as a doorstop and nudges it into place with her foot as we come in.
The bartender is inconsolable, wiping her eyes between orders and asking each customer what day it is before she pours their drink.
She pats the side of the flatbed truck twice before she gets in, like she's thanking it for waiting.
She presses her palm against the tree’s lumpy bark and waits a few seconds before nodding like it told her something.
She scrapes the last bit out of the roasted bone and sets it aside carefully like she might need it again later.
At the hotel desk she hands over her ID and, without being asked, quietly signs the line at the bottom of the check-in form that no one else seems to have.
She picks up a small bag of manure at the garden center and asks if it’s from a calm horse or a nervous one.
She stirs the batter slowly, counting each turn under her breath until she reaches twenty-three, then stops no matter how it looks.
She keeps wiping the waxy brim of her hat on the inside of her sleeve every few minutes.
She lines up the camping stove fuel canisters by expiration date and refuses to use the newest one.
She knocks twice on her own doorstep before unlocking the door.
She pulls out her vaccination card and glances at it before deciding what to order.
She turns the plum over in her palm and holds it to her ear for a second before taking a bite.
She coughs into her sleeve and says she’ll keep this one instead of passing it along.
She sets a pair of hot tweezers on the table between us and blows on them before using them to pluck a stray thread from her sleeve.

scene: We're at a small Portuguese grocery checkout and she separates her coins into neat little groups before handing them over, counting them in a whisper like she's trying not to wake them up.
She drops blueberries onto the counter one by one until one lands wrong and then quietly starts over from the beginning.
She wanders through the farmers market, only stepping on the darker tiles between stalls.
She rewrites her to-do list at the end of each day, keeping every task she already finished.
She flings the last fry out the car window for the birds before she takes a bite of her own.
She pounds the punching bag and quietly apologizes to it after every combination.
She hits the elevator button exactly seven times before letting it light.
She misspells her own name the same wrong way every time she signs anything.
She latches the front door, then quietly says "stay" to it before we walk away.
She crosses the street back and forth three times before going into the coffee shop.
She calls the bank to switch her mortgage and writes the representative’s name three times in three different notebooks before continuing.
She keeps talking to me while she casually takes apart the smoke detector over her head, placing each piece in her pocket.
She drinks her iced coffee through the straw in short, precise pulls, counting each one quietly to herself.
She throws stones crisply into the river, saying a different apology for each one even though no one’s around.
She always starts crossing the street a second before the signal changes, like she's keeping time with something just ahead of it.
She steers the car side to side in a perfectly even pattern down the empty street.
In the middle of making dinner, she suddenly starts running the kitchen like a drill sergeant, calling out times for each step.
She answers even simple questions in full, neatly structured paragraphs, out loud.
She bleaches the same t-shirt over and over, stopping only after the seventh round every time.
She jokes sullenly while we wait in line, delivering each punchline like an apology.
Her humor is very old-fashioned, she only laughs at jokes if they rhyme.
Her voice always rises at the end of every sentence like she’s asking a question, even when she’s telling you something she already knows.
Her opinions get so fiery she sets a two-minute timer before she’ll say them out loud.
Her presence is a little awkward, like even standing still she keeps lightly bumping her shoulder against the doorframe she already walked through.
Her humor is always slightly misremembered versions of jokes everyone knows, like she tells them with one key detail swapped.
She keeps her answers short because she says she only has so many words she can use in a day.
Her voice has a calm, medicinal tone, and she answers like she's reading a dosage label, adding exact times and amounts.
Her laugh is sharp and sour, like she's tasted something off, and she always says sorry right after it.
Her humor turns everything into a joke, even while we're filling out a form she keeps asking what the punchline is.
